::: {.project-detail}

::: {.project-hook}
Bizkit asks a deceptively simple question: **how can economics become interesting before it becomes difficult?**
:::

<p class="venture-status"><strong>Current practice:</strong> one story each week, usually on Sunday, published in English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and German.</p>

## Why it began

Economics is often introduced through definitions. Students meet elasticity, adverse selection, or opportunity cost before they have a reason to care about them.

That order never felt natural to me. I was drawn to economics because it explained decisions I could already observe: why a company changed its price, why two firms valued the same deal differently, or why a policy produced an unintended response.

Bizkit reverses the conventional sequence. It starts with the story.

## An inheritance—and a different choice

::: {.personal-origin-copy}
Engineering is woven through my family across generations—from my parents and grandparents to my great-grandparents. I was also born on the birthday of Sir M. Visvesvaraya, one of India’s most celebrated engineers. My family reasonably imagined that I would continue the pattern.

Instead, I became fascinated by economics: not a rejection of the systems-thinking I inherited, but a decision to apply it to people, incentives, firms, and markets. I opened Bizkit with that irony because it explains something central about the project. It is where an engineering inheritance meets the subject I chose for myself.
:::
:::

## The method

Every piece follows a common path:

1. A real company, decision, or market outcome
2. The detail that makes the outcome surprising
3. A question the reader now wants answered
4. The economic concept that makes the story legible
5. A return to the original decision with a stronger mental model

The project is partly educational and partly diagnostic. If I cannot explain an idea without relying on its textbook definition, I probably do not understand it well enough.

## What writing changed

I used to think writing presented finished thought. Repeated revision changed that belief.

A sentence that feels awkward often reveals an argument that is still unclear. A transition that refuses to work can expose two ideas that do not actually connect. Writing slowly enough makes assumptions visible.

Bizkit therefore became more than a collection of articles. It became a way to test my own understanding while making economics more accessible to another student.

## If I extended it today

I would keep the story-first structure but make the reader more active: short decisions, interactive cases, or simulations in which a concept emerges from a choice rather than an explanation. The purpose would remain unchanged—curiosity before instruction.

## Community-service direction

I intend to take this story-first, multilingual approach into government schools. That outreach has not happened yet, so the site makes no participation or impact claim. A field-notes and photograph module is reserved but will remain hidden until visits occur and the necessary school and student permissions are secured.
